title: Counting Style: The First Stylometrists
description: From De Morgan's hunch to Mendenhall's word curves and the naming of stylometry

concepts.title: De Morgan's Hunch and Mendenhall's Word Spectrum
concepts.contentHtml:
The idea that you can measure style is older than the computer. In 1851 the English mathematician Augustus De Morgan proposed that average word length might be used to settle questions of disputed authorship.1 Thirty-six years later the American physicist and meteorologist Thomas Corwin Mendenhall, of the Ohio State University, put the hunch to work in the journal Science, in a paper published on 11 March 1887.2

His method needed no judgement at all, only patience. Take 1,000 consecutive words, sort them by how many letters each has, and plot the counts: letters along the bottom, words per thousand up the side. Joined up, the points form what Mendenhall called a word spectrum or characteristic curve. In his first thousand words of Thackeray's Vanity Fair, three-letter words led with 232, ahead of 187 four-letter words and 169 two-letter words. The next thousand words drew a curve that differed, but agreed surprisingly well.

The bet underneath was psychological. Mendenhall assumed that unconscious habits persist, so an author's peculiarities would show up with such regularity that the curve could identify a writer, at least by exclusion. He judged that about 100,000 words would be necessary and sufficient for a stable curve.3 His early counts turned up some striking results:

  • Among writers of English the three-letter word was the most frequent, with one exception: John Stuart Mill, whose fondness for prepositional phrases made two-letter words such as in, on, to and of his commonest.4
  • Edward Atkinson gave a talk to college alumni and then gave the same talk to working men, deliberately using short, simple words.5 The two speeches read very differently, yet their curves were strikingly alike.
  • Someone once sent Mendenhall a bare column of numbers on a strip of paper. He plotted it and recognised the Latin of Caesar.

Notice the asymmetry he built in. Very different curves would be strong evidence against a shared author, but matching curves would prove much less, because two writers might happen to share a curve. That logic, better at ruling out than ruling in, still runs through the field.

concepts.title: Shakespeare, Bacon and the Counting Machine
concepts.contentHtml:
For more than ten years after 1887, people urged Mendenhall to point his method at the most famous authorship quarrel of all: did Francis Bacon write Shakespeare? The labour was beyond any volunteer. Then Augustus Heminway of Boston offered to pay for the work, which meant counting and classifying nearly two million words.

Two women from Worcester, Massachusetts, Mrs Richard Mitchell and Miss Amy C. Whitman, did the counting with a simple machine Mendenhall had built. One called out the letter count of each word in order ("five", "two", "three") while the other pressed the button marked with that number. The work was so exhausting that it could not be kept up for more than three to five hours a day.

Mendenhall reported the results in Popular Science Monthly in 1901. About 400,000 words of Shakespeare were counted and classified. His average word was a trifle under four letters long, and his most frequent word length was four letters, something Mendenhall had never met before; the counters said they could recognise Shakespeare by the run of words alone. Bacon's curve, built from nearly 200,000 words of his history of Henry VII, The Advancement of Learning and his essays, looked strikingly different. Ben Jonson, like most writers, favoured three-letter words. Then came Christopher Marlowe, and something close to a sensation: in the characteristic curve of his plays, Marlowe agreed with Shakespeare about as well as Shakespeare agreed with himself.

Mendenhall himself was careful. Even if Bacon was excluded, he wrote, the method could never do more than direct inquiry or suspicion. Now read the experiment with a critic's eye. Bacon's samples were prose histories and essays; Shakespeare's were mostly verse drama. Mendenhall admitted that no author had written enough in several forms to settle whether prose and poetry share a curve, although Shakespeare's four-letter habit was just as strong in his narrative poems as in his plays. A difference between two curves might reflect genre rather than hand. Comparing like with like became one of the field's first rules.

concepts.title: Stylometry Gets a Name
concepts.contentHtml:
The word itself came from Plato scholarship. In 1897 the Polish philosopher Wincenty Lutosławski published The Origin and Growth of Plato's Logic, which aimed to establish the order in which Plato wrote his dialogues by tracking how his style changed.1 He counted features such as rare words, sentence length and the ratios of nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs.2 Other scholars had already used such statistics on Plato, but Lutosławski proposed basic rules to make the method sound, and he christened it stylometry. Reviewing the book in 1899, the historian of science Paul Tannery was guarded about the rules but granted that stylometry would be invaluably helpful if it were grounded scientifically.3

Two questions were already in play: chronology (when did this author write this?) and attribution (who wrote this?). Both rest on one premise, which the computational linguist Patrick Juola states simply: language is a set of choices, and writers tend to fall into habitual ones. His example is a salad fork. It sits to the left of the plate, or on the left, or at the left, or to the left side of the plate: the same fork in the same place, at least four phrasings, and no obvious social or cognitive reason to prefer one. Yet much of this apparently free variation is fairly stable for an individual, so a model of someone's choices can be built from documents they have written.4

Statisticians joined in slowly. In his later years George Udny Yule applied statistics to literary style and published The Statistical Study of Literary Vocabulary in 1944.5 Without computers, though, every count was done by hand, which kept features crude and samples small. Expert judgement still dominated. As the stylometrist Mike Kestemont observes, earlier attribution was often based on checklists of stylistic features that scholars extracted from known oeuvres, and because those checklists were rarely documented, which features made the list seemed a matter of scholarly taste.6 Replacing taste with explicit, repeatable counts was the field's founding ambition. The next lesson shows the study that achieved it.

title: The Federalist Papers: Mosteller and Wallace
description: How twelve disputed essays, the word upon and Bayes' theorem launched modern attribution

concepts.title: Publius and the Twelve Disputed Papers
concepts.contentHtml:
Between October 1787 and May 1788, a series of essays urging New Yorkers to ratify the new United States Constitution appeared under a single pseudonym, Publius.1 The 85 papers of The Federalist were written by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay. Anonymity suited politically sensitive writing, but it left a puzzle that lasted 150 years.

The authors made it worse. In 1804, two days before the duel in which he was killed, Hamilton wrote a note claiming 63 of the 85 papers and left it with a friend.2 Ten years later Madison said that 12 of the papers on Hamilton's list were his.3 The historian Douglass Adair, in a famous 1944 article, explained that neither man had wanted his share known in his lifetime, and Adair himself concluded that Madison wrote all of the disputed papers.4 When the statisticians Frederick Mosteller and David L. Wallace took up the problem, the accepted division of the 77 essays that first appeared in newspapers was this:

  • Jay: five papers, Nos. 2, 3, 4, 5 and 64.
  • Hamilton: 43 papers. Madison: 14 papers.
  • Disputed between Hamilton and Madison: 12 papers, Nos. 49 to 58, 62 and 63.5
  • Joint: Nos. 18, 19 and 20, where the question is how much each man contributed.

Style looked hopeless too. Both men were masters of the popular Spectator style of writing, complicated and oratorical. In 1941 Frederick Williams and Frederick Mosteller counted sentence lengths in the undisputed papers and got means of 34.55 words for Hamilton and 34.59 for Madison, with average standard deviations of 19.2 and 20.3.6 On some measures, Mosteller and Wallace wrote, the two authors were practically twins.

That failure carries the first lesson of the case. A good marker must separate the candidates you actually have, and the most obvious features of a style, such as sentence length, may not separate them at all. The search had to move to something less obvious.

concepts.title: Upon, Whilst and a Storm of Confetti
concepts.contentHtml:
Mosteller, of Harvard, and Wallace, of the University of Chicago, began with a warning. The topic written about heavily influences the rate at which a word is used: in an essay on the armed forces you expect war often, in one on voting rarely.1 They called such words contextual and regarded them as dangerous for discrimination. Filler words such as an, of and upon, along with articles, prepositions and conjunctions generally, gave fairly stable rates.

The star was upon. Hamilton used it about three times per thousand words and Madison about once in six thousand, and Mosteller and Wallace called it the best single discriminator they had ever discovered.2 Adair had told them that while and whilst separated the two men quite well; in Patrick Juola's later summary, Hamilton never wrote whilst and Madison never wrote while.3 Other markers were subtler. Both men used by, but Madison consistently used it about twice as often.4

Choosing the words was itself a statistical trap, because a word picked for discriminating well in one sample may simply have been lucky there. Mosteller and Wallace pooled candidates from several screening studies into 165 words, then cut these to 30 words in five groups before the disputed papers were analysed.5 Along the way they kept only words whose rates were homogeneous across Madison's papers, and dropped personal pronouns and auxiliary verbs as potentially contextual. Fixing the word list before looking at the disputed papers kept the test honest, a discipline every attribution study still needs.

The counting was physical. They cut paper copies of the essays into individual words, then alphabetised and counted them.6 In their book they recalled that during this operation a deep breath created a storm of confetti and a permanent enemy.7 Computers soon took over: part of the work ran at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Computation Center, with programmers handling both the word counts and the high-speed calculations.

concepts.title: Bayes at Scale
concepts.contentHtml:
The main study was Bayesian, and that, as much as the verdict, made it famous. Bayes' theorem in odds form says that your final odds for Madison over Hamilton equal your initial odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio: how much more probable the observed word counts are if Madison wrote the paper than if Hamilton did. Mosteller and Wallace pointed out a reassuring consequence. If the likelihood ratio is large enough, or small enough, wide changes in the initial odds change the final probabilities only slightly.1 It hardly matters how strongly a historian started out believing in Hamilton.

The hard part was the likelihood. Any single word is a rare event at any given spot, so a natural first model for its count is the Poisson distribution, whose variance equals its mean. For an, any and upon it fitted Hamilton's counts in 200-word blocks rather well, but for may and his the counts were too spread out.2 The cure was the negative binomial. Suppose a writer uses a word at a Poisson rate within each piece of writing, but that the rate itself drifts from piece to piece following a gamma distribution;3 the counts across many pieces then follow a negative binomial, with mean \(\lambda\) and variance \(\lambda(1+\lambda/\kappa)\). The extra term measures how far a word departs from Poisson behaviour. Because the rates themselves were uncertain, Mosteller and Wallace also gave them prior distributions, estimated from a pool of words not used for discrimination.

The verdict was clear. Madison rather than Hamilton wrote all 12 of the disputed papers.4 The weakest case was No. 55, yet even there they estimated the odds for Madison at 100 to 1.5 For the statistician William Kruskal, the Federalist gave a specific, fascinating historical context in which to compare Bayesian and frequentist modes of statistical analysis.6 It is still a standard test case for machine-learning methods, and some later research suggests that Hamilton and Madison may have co-written more of the Federalist than anyone suspected.

title: Function Words and Burrows's Delta
description: Why the, of and upon betray authors, and how Delta turns them into a distance

concepts.title: Why Small Words Carry Big Signals
concepts.contentHtml:
Mosteller and Wallace's lasting gift was a choice of evidence. Earlier attribution leaned on features that struck expert readers as typical of an author, and those features were often rare: an uncommon noun, a pet phrase. Rare features cause two problems. They are often tied to a specific genre or topic, and because they are striking, imitators and followers can copy them.1 Mosteller and Wallace moved attention from a language's low-frequency features to its high-frequency ones, which tend to be2 function words.

Linguists divide words into an open class of content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives), which is large and grows every day, and a closed class of function words (prepositions, particles, determiners), which is small and hard to expand: try inventing a new preposition. Function words carry little meaning on their own but are used constantly. Less than 0.04% of our vocabulary accounts for over half of the words we actually use in daily speech.3 That gives three advantages at once:

  • Frequency: even a short text contains hundreds of them, so their rates can be estimated reliably.
  • Topic independence: everyone writing in the same language and period uses the same function words, whatever the subject.
  • Low awareness: in Efstathios Stamatatos's phrase they are used in a largely unconscious manner, which also makes them very hard for a forger to copy.4

John Burrows's 1987 book Computation into Criticism, a study of Jane Austen's novels, showed critics how much these little words could reveal.5 In the 1990s a rival appeared: character n-grams, overlapping strings of letters such as the four characters "n th" spanning "in the". Since work by Kjell in 1994, character n-grams have often been the best-performing features of all, even though they look meaningless.6 Kestemont likens the use of both to a sort of black magic. His explanation is that n-grams capture grammatical pieces of words, such as endings, that behave just like function words, and he proposes calling the whole category functors.

concepts.title: Delta, Step by Step
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2002 John Burrows introduced the measure that became the workhorse of literary stylometry: Delta. It compares a disputed text with many candidate authors at once; his original paper used about 25.1 The recipe is short:

  • Take the n most frequent words of the whole corpus, mostly function words. Choosing n is something of a dark art; studies have used anywhere from 100 to 1,000.2
  • Compute each word's relative frequency in each candidate's writing and in the disputed text.
  • Standardise each frequency as a z-score: subtract the word's mean and divide by its standard deviation. Burrows did this so that every word counts as a marker of potentially equal power, and the and of cannot drown out the rest.3
  • For each candidate, average the absolute differences between the disputed text's z-scores and the candidate's. That average is Delta.
  • The smallest Delta marks the most similar, and so the most likely, author.

Try it where you know the answer. Federalist 64 is agreed to be John Jay's. In a Programming Historian tutorial, François Dominic Laramée ran Delta on 30 common words against five candidate corpora. Jay scored 1.53, ahead of Madison at 1.61 and Hamilton at 1.77, so the method passed its test.4 Intriguingly, the disputed papers taken as a group scored 1.54, almost as close as Jay.

Delta is a so-called lazy learner: it builds no model, it simply measures distance, which makes it transparent and easy to rerun. It has proved robust across genres and languages.5 It also comes with a sensible stability check. If a small change in n flips the attribution, the test is not giving meaningful evidence about your case.6 A careful study therefore reports results across many settings, not just the one that gives the hoped-for answer.

concepts.title: Why Delta Works, and Its Rivals
concepts.contentHtml:
For years Delta worked better than anyone could explain. Shlomo Argamon showed that its second step is the Manhattan distance between two points in a space with one dimension per word, and he proposed a Quadratic Delta, equivalent to Euclidean distance, that can be derived from a probabilistic model.1 In 2011 Peter Smith and W. Aldridge suggested measuring the angle between the two vectors instead: Cosine Delta. A comparison on English, German and French novels found that Burrows's Delta remains a strong contender but is outperformed quite clearly by Cosine Delta, which also avoids the usual drop in performance when very many words are used.2

Why should the angle matter? Stefan Evert, Fotis Jannidis and colleagues ran controlled experiments that separated the scaling of features from the distance measure. Their answer, published in 2017: vector normalisation, rescaling each text's profile to a length of 1, which the cosine measure does implicitly, is the decisive factor.3 They then tested two explanations:

  • The outlier hypothesis: normalisation helps by taming a few extreme z-scores. It failed, because normalisation hardly reduced the number of extreme values.4
  • The key-profile hypothesis: the authorial signal lies in the pattern of which words a writer over-uses and under-uses, not in how extreme the values are. It held. Vectors reduced to just +1, 0 and -1, for above-average, unremarkable and below-average frequencies, performed almost as well as full normalisation.5

The lesson generalises. An author is a profile of small leanings spread across hundreds of common words, not a few telltale tics, which is also why such profiles are hard to fake. Free tools now package these methods. The R package stylo, by Maciej Eder, Jan Rybicki and Mike Kestemont, offers Delta and its variants alongside classifiers such as support vector machines, plus6 culling, which keeps only words that appear in a set share of the texts, and bootstrap consensus trees, which combine many analyses over different word bands so that only stable groupings survive.

title: Unmasking Robert Galbraith
description: The 2013 Rowling case, what four tests can and cannot show, and the unmasking method

concepts.title: The Cuckoo's Calling Case
concepts.contentHtml:
In July 2013 London's Sunday Times revealed that J.K. Rowling had written the detective novel1 The Cuckoo's Calling under the pen name Robert Galbraith. The paper had received an anonymous tip via Twitter.2 Before confronting her, it sought the help of two scholars who had built software for authorship attribution: Peter Millican of Oxford University and Patrick Juola of Duquesne University.3

Juola set conditions. He needed clean, machine-readable copies of the mystery novel and of something comparable that was undisputedly Rowling's, and comparable books by other writers, called distractor authors, to show how much ordinary variation looks like. He received Rowling's The Casual Vacancy and three British crime novels: Ruth Rendell's The St. Zita Society, P.D. James's The Private Patient and Val McDermid's The Wire in the Blood.4 He cut The Cuckoo's Calling into 11 chunks of 1,000 lines and, with his JGAAP software and a cosine distance, compared each chunk with each candidate on four kinds of feature:

  • Word-length distribution: six sections closest to Rowling, five to James.5
  • The 100 most common words: four Rowling-like, four McDermid-like, three split between James and Rendell.
  • Character 4-grams, strings of four adjacent characters: eight sections closest to McDermid, three to Rowling.
  • Word bigrams, pairs of adjacent words: nine Rowling-like, two McDermid-like.6

No single test was decisive, and one favoured McDermid. But nothing at all pointed to Rendell, only one unreliable test suggested James, and Rowling was the only author who came first or second on every feature. That consistency across very different kinds of evidence is what made the result worth acting on. The Sunday Times approached Rowling's agent and asked directly whether she had written the book. Less than a day later, Rowling confirmed through a spokesman that she had.7

concepts.title: Suggestive, Not Proof
concepts.contentHtml:
Juola was careful about what his tests showed. Out of four candidates, Rowling was always in the more similar half. A randomly chosen author would land in that half on any one test about half the time, so passing all four tests is roughly a one-in-16 event, and even that assumes the tests are independent, which Juola admitted was handwaving.1 Nothing in the analysis, he wrote, constituted proof; it was at best suggestive or perhaps indicative.2 Had the author been long dead, with no confession possible, it is the kind of result that would be argued about in the journals for decades.3

Two structural limits sit behind that caution. First, this was a closed-set problem: the method picks the best match among the candidates supplied, and Rowling could only win because the newspaper had named her. The book could just as well have been written by someone who, by accident or design, wrote like Rowling. Second, the distractors mattered. The Sunday Times had found authors similar in gender, dialect, genre and period, which made the comparison fair.4 Choose distractors carelessly and almost any candidate will look distinctive. Clean e-books helped too, since many historical studies start from scanned or retyped texts of poor quality.

The harder and more common problem is authorship verification: you suspect one author and have no complete list of alternatives. Moshe Koppel and colleagues put it neatly. To decide whether a text is by Shakespeare or Marlowe, you need only their known works. To decide whether it is by Shakespeare or not, you must assemble a representative sample of not-Shakespeare, which is very difficult, if not impossible.5 Verification must also separate shallow differences, such as a change of topic or a deliberate change of manner, from the deeper differences that mark different people.

The Galbraith case has since become a teaching standard: the stylo package for R ships a Galbraith dataset so that students can rerun an attribution of their own.

concepts.title: Unmasking: How Deep Is the Difference?
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2007 Koppel, Jonathan Schler and Elisheva Bonchek-Dokow proposed an answer to verification, and it begins with a trap. Take Nathaniel Hawthorne's The House of the Seven Gables and try to tell it apart from known works by Herman Melville, James Fenimore Cooper and Hawthorne himself, using the 250 most frequent words. A standard classifier separates the book from each author, Hawthorne included, with cross-validation accuracy above 98%.1 Conclude that none of them wrote it, and you are wrong: Hawthorne did.2

The reason is that a small number of features, often words tied to plot, setting or character, do all the work of distinguishing two books by the same author. So unmasking removes them. Train a classifier, delete the most strongly weighted features on each side, retrain, and repeat. For two different authors, accuracy stays high and falls slowly, because their differences run through hundreds of words. For the same author, accuracy drops suddenly and dramatically after a few rounds: once the superficial markers are gone, the two books are hard to tell apart.3 Same-author and different-author curves look so unlike each other that the curves themselves can be classified, and the authors reported very high accuracy on verification tests.

Then a real mystery. Ben Ish Chai, the leading rabbinic scholar in Baghdad in the late 19th century, left one collection of legal responsa under his own name, Rav Pe'alim, with 509 documents, and another, Torah Lishmah, with 524, which he claimed to have found in an archive.4 Historians had long believed he wrote it himself, and he may have altered his style to hide that. An impostors step first eliminated four other authors of responsa from the same region and period. Unmasking then produced a curve for Ben Ish Chai far below the others, affirming the historians' consensus.5 Tellingly, the strongest distinguishing features, the first to be removed, were different standard sign-offs in the two collections, which could be deliberate disguise or simply a change over time.

title: Shakespeare's Collaborators
description: Fletcher, Peele and Middleton, Marlowe's credit on Henry VI, and a retracted elegy

concepts.title: Co-authors in the Canon
concepts.contentHtml:
The Elizabethan and Jacobean theatre ran on collaboration, and Shakespeare's shared plays are stylometry's oldest proving ground. In 1850 the British scholar James Spedding published an article attributing several scenes of Henry VIII to John Fletcher.1 His evidence was metrical: the ratio of verse lines ending on a stressed syllable to lines ending with an extra unstressed syllable. Across the play's scenes the values were strongly bimodal, as if two writers had shared it.2

Petr Plecháč put Spedding's division to a machine-learning test in a study first posted in 2019. He trained a support vector machine on scenes from plays by Shakespeare, Fletcher and Philip Massinger, using two feature sets together: the 500 most frequent words and the 500 most frequent rhythmic types, the patterns of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line. Instead of classifying whole scenes, he used rolling attribution, sliding a window through the text so that a change of writer could fall in the middle of a scene. On known plays the combined models misattributed only 10 groups of lines out of 4,412 when telling Shakespeare from Fletcher.3 For Henry VIII they largely confirmed Spedding and made Massinger's participation rather unlikely, but they placed one hand-over at line 2200 rather than at line 2081, in agreement with earlier work by Thomas Merriam.4

Other partnerships have been argued just as hard. In his book Shakespeare, Co-Author, Brian Vickers used evidence from vocabulary, syntax, verse style and rhetoric to argue that:

  • George Peele wrote all of Act 1 and the first two scenes of Act 2 of Titus Andronicus.
  • Thomas Middleton composed nine scenes of Timon of Athens, about a third of the play.5
  • George Wilkins wrote the first two acts of Pericles.
  • John Fletcher co-wrote Henry VIII and The Two Noble Kinsmen.

A reviewer noted that few Shakespeare scholars would be stunned by the Fletcher and Wilkins claims, while the Peele and Middleton shares were much more inflammatory.6 Note what the newer studies add: not just a yes or no for each scene, but an estimate of exactly where one writer stops and another begins.

concepts.title: Marlowe in Henry VI
concepts.contentHtml:
In October 2016 Oxford University Press announced that its New Oxford Shakespeare, edited by Gary Taylor, John Jowett, Terri Bourus and Gabriel Egan, would credit Christopher Marlowe as a co-author of all three Henry VI plays.1 It was the first time a major publishing house had formally named Marlowe as a co-author.2 Taylor stressed that this was not a claim that Marlowe was the real author of Shakespeare. It was ordinary Elizabethan collaboration, in which a scenario setting out the plot could be divided between writers. People had suspected Marlowe's hand in these plays since the 1790s, Taylor said, but there had been no way to test it until Shakespeare entered the epoch of big data.3

The case drew on several kinds of evidence:

  • Vocabulary: 2009 research by Hugh Craig and Arthur Kinney comparing the vocabulary of the Henry VI plays with plays known to be Marlowe's, and a 2015 article by John Nance on the prose of Part 2.4
  • Rare collocations: Taylor's example is glory droopeth. Neither word is unusual, but the pair occurs in a disputed passage of Part 1 and, among all the plays of the period, only in one other place: a play by Marlowe.5 One such pair proves nothing; many unusual combinations clustered in one passage suggest a second writer.
  • Word adjacency networks: a study by Egan with a team of mathematicians from the University of Pennsylvania.

The last method changes the question. In a word adjacency network (WAN), developed by Santiago Segarra, Mark Eisen and Alejandro Ribeiro, the nodes are function words and the directed edges stand for the likelihood of finding one function word shortly after another.6 Each author's network is treated as the transition probabilities of a Markov chain, and networks are compared by their relative entropy. In benchmark tests, attribution accuracy exceeded that of methods based on word frequencies alone, and combining the two did better still.7 Delta asks how often you use the; a WAN asks what you put after it. Two writers can use function words at the same rates and still arrange them differently.

concepts.title: Contested Hands and a Cautionary Elegy
concepts.contentHtml:
Not everyone was convinced. Carol Rutter of the University of Warwick told the BBC she would be very surprised if Marlowe was one of Shakespeare's collaborators.1 She suggested that the young Shakespeare worked with actors who had Marlowe very much in their heads and voices, and that they carried his influence into the plays. Statistical critics went further. In 2020 Ros Barber argued that the word adjacency method behind the attribution had not been independently tested, that sections designated as Shakespeare's were often not detected as his by the method's own definitions, and that its high claimed success rates rested on a flawed validation process known as overfitting.2 She concluded that the key studies should be set aside. Pervez Rizvi had published earlier criticisms in 2018. The credit stands in the edition; the argument is live.

Why such caution? Consider A Funerall Elegye, a poem published in 1612 in memory of William Peter and signed only W.S. In a 1989 monograph, Elegy by W.S.: A Study in Attribution, Donald Foster of Vassar College argued that Shakespeare wrote it.3 When the media took up the claim in 1996, Foster became a celebrity literary detective, and he went on to identify the journalist Joe Klein as the anonymous author of the political novel Primary Colors.4 The Norton Shakespeare even included the elegy.5 Brian Vickers then argued in detail, feature by feature, that the evidence for Shakespeare proved nothing, and built a case for the Jacobean dramatist John Ford. After Gilles Monsarrat independently argued for Ford, Foster conceded in June 2002, writing that no one who cannot rejoice in the discovery of his own mistakes deserves to be called a scholar.6

The general lesson is to weigh negative evidence. Vickers made the same charge against Gary Taylor's attribution of the lyric Shall I Die?: Taylor failed to check his verbal parallels against the verse of other poets writing between 1590 and 1620.7 A parallel with Shakespeare means little until you know how common it was in everyone else.

title: Who Is Elena Ferrante?
description: A money trail, a shared corpus of 150 novels, and the ethics of unmasking a pen name

concepts.title: A Pen Name and a Paper Trail
concepts.contentHtml:
Elena Ferrante's first novel appeared in Italy in 1992, and the four novels of the Neapolitan quartet (2011 to 2014) made her an international phenomenon. Her small Rome-based publisher, Edizioni e/o, kept her real identity secret for more than 25 years.1 Ferrante gave interviews through the publisher and gathered letters, interviews and autobiographical writing in Frantumaglia, while warning there that she would lie when necessary to shield herself.2 Before her first book came out, she promised her publishers she would be their least expensive author, sparing them even her presence.

On 2 October 2016 the journalist Claudio Gatti published an investigation, in Il Sole 24 Ore and in English in The New York Review of Books, that ignored the novels' text altogether. He followed the money. Real-estate records and payments from the publisher, he argued, pointed to Anita Raja, a Rome-based translator of German literature who had worked with Edizioni e/o for many years and is married to the novelist Domenico Starnone.3 In 2014 Raja's compensation increased by almost 50%, and in 2015 it grew by more than 150%, to about seven times what she had received in 2010, closely tracking the publisher's Ferrante-driven revenues.4

Gatti also listed the earlier, text-based guesses. A decade before, at the request of the writer Luigi Galella, physicists and mathematicians at La Sapienza University in Rome had concluded there was a high probability that Starnone wrote the books.5 The Dante scholar Marco Santagata had named the historian Marcella Marmo. The reaction to Gatti was fierce. The publisher Sandro Ferri called such an article an invasion of privacy, both the publishers' and Ferrante's, and neither Raja nor Starnone responded to Gatti's requests for comment.6

Notice what a money trail can and cannot show. It can show who was paid. It cannot show who wrote the sentences, or whether one person wrote them alone. That second question is the one stylometry can address.

concepts.title: The Padua Experiment
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2016 Arjuna Tuzzi and Michele Cortelazzo, at the University of Padua, built a corpus of 150 Italian novels published in the previous 30 years by 40 different authors, chosen with the main hypotheses about Ferrante in mind.1 Then they did something unusual: they shared the data with international experts and invited them to apply their own methods. Maciej Eder and Jan Rybicki, Patrick Juola, Vittorio Loreto's team, George Mikros, Pierre Ratinaud and Jacques Savoy all took part, and the results were presented at the workshop Drawing Elena Ferrante's Profile in Padua on 7 September 2017.2 One shared corpus made the methods directly comparable.

The methods differed. The answer did not.

  • Tuzzi and Cortelazzo found Ferrante among the most original authors in the corpus, standing in splendid isolation from the other women writers. The novelist closest to her lexical profile was Domenico Starnone, and the similarity held when they measured distance using grammatical words only, so it was not a matter of shared settings or plots.3
  • Savoy ran Delta on each of Ferrante's seven novels with seven sizes of feature set, on both word forms and lemmas: 98 experiments, with Starnone ranked first every time.4
  • Eder used rolling classification with a support vector machine on the 100 most frequent words, stepping through each novel 500 words at a time. With no single exception, every segment of every Ferrante novel was ascribed to Starnone.5
  • Juola compared the concepts authors use. Of 39 distractor authors, only Michela Murgia and Starnone showed no significant differences from Ferrante.6

Juola added the standard warning. This is a closed-set result: if you allow none of the above as an answer, all that has been shown is that Ferrante writes like Starnone and Murgia.7 Tuzzi and Cortelazzo noted a deeper limit. If the real author published only as Ferrante, or wrote under their own name only in other genres, a corpus of novels cannot find them.

concepts.title: One Author, Two People, or a Virtual Third?
concepts.contentHtml:
If the stylometry points to Starnone and the money points to Raja, both may be partly right. Several Padua contributors explored how that could be.

  • The virtual author. Eder recalled a study of two medieval Latin visions ascribed to Hildegard of Bingen. Works she wrote with her secretary, Guibert of Gembloux, formed a distinct profile that was not a simple mix of the two styles: a virtual third author.1 On the Synergy Hypothesis, associated with Pennebaker, a jointly written work may resemble one partner's style, or neither.
  • The invisible partner. Rybicki had studied two novels openly co-written by the Polish writer Jacek Dehnel and his partner, the translator Piotr Tarczyński. The stylometric signal was exclusively Dehnel's, although Rybicki knew Tarczyński had taken part.2 Raja's stylometric invisibility, he suggested, might be linked to her profession, and Ferrante could plausibly be a joint effort of Raja and Starnone.3
  • Other genres. Tuzzi, Cortelazzo and Mikros compared the non-fiction fragments of Frantumaglia with essays, articles and interviews by other writers. Their preliminary results suggested more than one author, seemingly at least one man and one woman, from Naples and over 60 years old; they pointed to Starnone and Raja and seemed to rule out Marmo.4

So the strongest defensible conclusion is narrower than the headlines. Ferrante's novels are closer in style to Starnone's than to those of any other novelist tested, and the books may be the work of some form of cooperation.5 Rybicki noted that readers, translators and publishers who insist the author must be a woman are not necessarily contradicted by the statistics.

There is also an ethical question. A pen name is a deliberate choice, and stylometry can override it. Rybicki, who took part, wrote that in his private opinion the sensational question of identity is infinitely less important than what happens when people write together.6 Before you run an attribution, ask who benefits from the answer and who bears its cost.

title: Distant Reading and the Age of Language Models
description: Moretti's distant reading, its critics, and what LLMs change for attribution and its limits

concepts.title: Distant Reading and Its Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
Stylometry counts words to find authors. In 2000 Franco Moretti asked what else counting could find. In his essay Conjectures on World Literature, in New Left Review, he admitted that, as a scholar of West European narrative between 1790 and 1930, he really worked only on its canonical fraction, which is not even one per cent of published literature.1 There are thirty thousand nineteenth-century British novels, perhaps forty, fifty or sixty thousand, and no one has read them or ever will.2 Reading more is no solution. Moretti proposed instead a little pact with the devil: we know how to read texts, now let us learn how not to read them.3 This is distant reading, in which distance is a condition of knowledge, letting you study units much smaller or much larger than the text,4 from devices and tropes to genres and whole systems.

His Stanford Literary Lab made the link to stylometry concrete. In its first pamphlet, Quantitative Formalism (2011), Sarah Allison, Ryan Heuser, Matthew Jockers, Moretti and Michael Witmore asked whether a computer could recognise literary genres with no human input. Their answer was fundamentally yes, but with many complications.5 Using the frequencies of the most common words and punctuation marks, the same features that betray authors, the clustering sorted most of Shakespeare's plays into tragedies, comedies, histories and late plays. Yet in the novels they kept running into the author signal: for Dickens, Brontë and Eliot, the pull of the author was much stronger than the pull of the genre.6

Critics pushed back hard. In Critical Inquiry in 2019, Nan Z. Da argued that computational literary analysis produces insights that are either robust and obvious or not obvious and not robust.7 Stanley Fish added that such projects dress up literary intuition in numbers.8 Defenders such as Katherine Bode replied that Da defines the field too narrowly, and Paul Barrett that computation enlarges the questions literary scholars are able to ask. Attribution sits slightly apart in this quarrel. Unlike many distant readings, it makes a claim that a confession, a manuscript or a letter can check.

concepts.title: Machines That Read for Authors
concepts.contentHtml:
Large language models change stylometry in two directions at once. They are new tools for attribution, and they are new authors to attribute.

On the tool side, Baixiang Huang, Canyu Chen and Kai Shu asked in 2024 whether LLMs can identify authorship without any task-specific training. Traditional studies depend on hand-crafted stylistic features, and state-of-the-art approaches use text embeddings from pretrained language models, but these typically need fine-tuning on labelled data, often degrade when moved to a new domain, and explain little.1 The study found LLMs proficient at both zero-shot verification and attribution among 10 or 20 candidate authors, and guiding them with explicit linguistic features let them explain their decisions.2 The same authors' survey sorts the new landscape into four problems: attributing human-written text, detecting LLM-generated text, attributing LLM-generated text, and attributing text that humans and LLMs wrote together.3 The last is the frontier, because co-writing with a model blurs the very idea of a single author.

On the other side, classic stylometry turns out to see machines rather clearly. James O'Sullivan of University College Cork used Burrows's Delta on short stories written to the same prompts by people and by GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama 70B, in a study published in 2025.4 The models' stories formed tight clusters, each with the uniform pattern of its own model, while the human stories were far more varied.5 GPT-4 wrote with even more consistency than GPT-3.5, which only rarely came close to human style.6 A 2026 preprint by Nasser Alsadhan asked GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet 3.5 to imitate Walt Whitman, William Wordsworth, Donald Trump and Barack Obama. The imitations remained highly detectable: a classifier trained on just eight stylometric features matched the accuracy of high-dimensional neural classifiers, and perplexity was the most discriminating feature.7

Notice the pattern. Models imitate the surface of a style well, but their outputs are more regular than people are, and regularity is exactly what frequency-based methods measure.

concepts.title: The Limits: Detectors, Disguise and Doubt
concepts.contentHtml:
Telling machine text from human text is far harder than separating a few models from a few writers. OpenAI withdrew its own AI text classifier on 20 July 2023, citing its low rate of accuracy.1 Many detectors rely on perplexity, how surprised a language model is by each next word, on the reasoning that machine text is predictable. But so is the writing of people with a narrower range of expression. Weixin Liang and colleagues tested seven widely used detectors on 91 TOEFL essays by non-native English speakers and 88 essays by US eighth-graders.2 The detectors classified the US essays accurately but labelled more than half the TOEFL essays as AI-generated, with an average false-positive rate of 61.3%.3

Detectors are also easy to evade. Kalpesh Krishna and colleagues built DIPPER, an 11-billion-parameter paraphrasing model. Paraphrasing AI text with it cut DetectGPT's detection accuracy from 70.3% to 4.6%, at a false-positive rate of 1%, without appreciably changing the meaning, and it also evaded watermarking and other detectors.4 Their proposed defence is different in kind: the provider keeps a database of everything its model has generated and checks a suspect text against it for similar meaning. A watermark, which softly nudges a model towards a secret, randomised set of green tokens,5 is another provenance approach that works only if the provider builds it in.

People can disguise themselves too. In 2012 Michael Brennan, Sadia Afroz and Rachel Greenstadt asked volunteers who were not professional writers, and who spent little time on the task, to hide their style or to imitate someone else's. Obfuscation reduced the attribution methods to the level of random guessing, and imitation succeeded up to 67% of the time. A language model can now do that rewriting for anyone in seconds.

Attribution works best with long texts, a closed and well-chosen candidate set, comparable genres and an author who is not trying to hide. It yields evidence, never a verdict. O'Sullivan, whose own study separated people from models, insists that stylometry has no place in judging authorship in education, because students' writing shifts with task, context and support.6
